content: 1. Mothers should be provided with practical support to help them initiate and establish breastfeeding, as well as to manage common breastfeeding challenges. This recommendation is based on moderate-quality evidence. 2. Mothers should be taught how to express breast milk to maintain lactation in cases where they are temporarily separated from their infants. This recommendation is supported by very low-quality evidence. 3. A systematic review comparing rooming-in (keeping mothers and infants together in the same room) versus separating them after birth identified only one study with 176 participants that met inclusion criteria. The evidence quality was moderate. 4. Additional analysis of non-randomized controlled trials on rooming-in versus separate care identified three studies measuring breastfeeding at 3–4 months of age. The evidence quality was very low. 5. The overall quality of evidence for rooming-in on critical outcomes is moderate. Details of the systematic review and findings are available in annexes. 6. A review reported that the median duration of any breastfeeding was 4 months, with no significant difference between rooming-in and separate care groups. Rooming-in was associated with more frequent feeding compared to scheduled feeding intervals in the separate care group. 7. Literature on mothers' preferences for rooming-in showed that most mothers preferred to room-in with their infants, although a significant proportion preferred not to room-in at night. This evidence has moderate confidence. 8. Health workers' perspectives on rooming-in varied. Some supported the practice, while others felt it was unnecessary. Many health workers offered separate care to allow mothers to rest. Neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) staff reported resource limitations preventing 24-hour rooming-in. 9. Resource implications for rooming-in include costs related to hospital infrastructure. Inadequate resources and space may lead to unsafe sleeping environments. NICUs are often not equipped for continuous rooming-in. 10. Facilities providing maternity and newborn services should enable mothers and infants to remain together and practice rooming-in throughout the day and night, except when infants require specialized medical care. This recommendation is based on moderate-quality evidence. 11. Demand feeding, where infants are fed in response to hunger and satiety cues, was reviewed. No eligible studies were found to compare demand feeding with scheduled feeding in term or preterm infants. Evidence quality is very low. 12. Mothers value demand feeding but often feel they need more support. Some mothers feel uncertain or anxious about interpreting their infants' hunger and feeding cues, particularly in NICU settings. 13. Health workers' views on demand feeding varied. Some were unaware of the concept, while others were uncomfortable promoting it due to traditional practices of scheduled feeding. In specialized units like NICUs, strict documentation of feeds is often required. 14. Resource implications for demand feeding are similar to those for rooming-in, including costs related to hospital infrastructure and potential space or equipment challenges. 15. Mothers should be supported to practice responsive feeding as part of nurturing care. This recommendation is based on very low-quality evidence. 16. Early and uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact between mothers and infants should be facilitated and encouraged as soon as possible after birth. This practice is supported by moderate-quality evidence. 17. All mothers should be supported to initiate breastfeeding as soon as possible after delivery. This recommendation is based on high-quality evidence. 18. Interventions supporting breastfeeding initiation immediately after birth have strong evidence for reducing mortality and improving breastfeeding outcomes beyond the hospital stay. 19. Early skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding initiation increase the likelihood of exclusive breastfeeding up to 3–6 months of life. 20. Mothers and infants who room-in together are almost twice as likely to exclusively breastfeed during their hospital stay. 21. Supporting mothers to form early, close relationships and feed their infants is highly valued by mothers and has significant benefits for both. 22. Health workers often report limited knowledge and confidence in supporting breastfeeding. Guidance on minimum support and addressing common breastfeeding problems is necessary. 23. Collaboration or referral may be needed to address complex breastfeeding challenges. 24. Focused and optimal immediate support for breastfeeding initiation in the first hours and days of life has long-term positive effects. 25. Skin-to-skin contact should ideally last for more than one hour and be encouraged for longer periods if well-tolerated by both mother and infant. 26. During early skin-to-skin contact, health-care personnel should observe and manage any signs of distress while ensuring safety. 27. Early breastfeeding initiation within the first hour after delivery has significant benefits. Feeding cues may appear within 15–20 minutes or later. 28. Mothers unable to initiate breastfeeding within the first hour should still be supported to breastfeed as soon as they are able, including those who deliver via cesarean section or have medical instability. 29. Mothers should be enabled to achieve effective breastfeeding, including proper positioning, responding to feeding cues, and expressing breast milk when needed. 30. Breast milk expression is often used to stimulate attachment and effective sucking during breastfeeding establishment, not just when mothers and infants are separated. 31. Mothers of infants in NICUs should be supported to have skin-to-skin contact, recognize their infants' cues, and express breast milk effectively soon after birth. 32. Feeding practices and additional needs of infants were informed by systematic reviews and qualitative evidence synthesis. Key questions and outcomes are detailed in annexes. 33. Resource use, feasibility, equity, and human rights issues were considered for all interventions. Specific resource implications are presented for each intervention.
